items.title: Hiring a Community Hall
items.context: A man phones a community centre to hire its hall for his mother's seventieth birthday party.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a community centre to book a room for a family party. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 6.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Good morning, Larkfield Community Centre, Janet speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Oh, hello. Um, I'm ringing about hiring one of your rooms for a party. It's for my mum - she's turning seventy, and we wanted to do something a bit special for her.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Oh, how lovely. Well, you've come to the right place, we do a lot of birthdays. Let me just take a few details first. Could I have your name?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, it's Daniel Cartwell.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Daniel... Cartwright, was that?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Everyone says that. No, it's Cartwell. C... A... R... T... W... E... double L.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: C, A, R, T, W, E, double L. Got it, thank you. And what sort of date were you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Well, her actual birthday is Wednesday the tenth of May, but obviously a weekday's no good for most people, so we were looking at the Saturday after that... the thirteenth.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Ah. I'm afraid the thirteenth has gone. We've got a wedding reception in all day. How about the following Saturday?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: So that'd be... the twentieth?

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: That's right. The twentieth is completely free at the moment.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Then let's go for that. My sister did say she couldn't make the thirteenth anyway, so it's probably for the best.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Lovely, I'll pencil you in. And roughly how many guests are you expecting?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That's the tricky bit. We sent out sixty invitations, but quite a few people are bringing partners, and Mum keeps adding cousins I've never heard of... so realistically we're planning for about eighty-five.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Eighty-five. Right, that does narrow things down. Our Willow Room is lovely, but it only takes forty-five, so that's out. The main hall holds two hundred...

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That sounds a bit enormous for us.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: It can feel rather empty with a smaller group, yes. So I'd suggest the Orchard Room. It takes up to a hundred, and it opens straight onto the garden, which is nice in May.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Oh, that sounds perfect. Mum's a keen gardener.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Now, the price. On a Saturday the standard rate is forty-five pounds an hour...

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Ah. Right.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: No, hang on, sorry, that's the main hall. I was looking at the wrong line. The Orchard Room is thirty-eight pounds an hour.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Thirty-eight. That's better than I expected. Is there a discount for people who live locally? Someone told me there was.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: There used to be, but the trustees stopped it last year, I'm afraid.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Never mind. And what time could we get in? We'd want to put decorations up.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: The room's free from midday, so you can come in any time after that, but the time you spend decorating does count towards the hire.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Then we'll be quick about it. Probably three o'clock until eleven.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Three till eleven. Now, as for what's included... tables and chairs, of course, and we can lend you white tablecloths at no extra charge. There's a fully equipped kitchen, with plates and cutlery for a hundred.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: And glasses?

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: We had a set of glasses, but so many got broken that we don't supply them any more. So you'd have to bring your own glasses, or hire some.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Right. I'll ask the caterers, they might have some.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 7 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Now, there are a few other things I should mention. Parking first.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, that'll matter. A lot of Mum's friends drive.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Well, the car park has forty spaces, and it doesn't shut at night, so nobody gets locked in. People used to need a permit to park there, but we got rid of that system a couple of years ago.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Great.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: The only thing is, there's a yoga class in the studio on Saturday evenings, and they normally take about a dozen of those spaces until half past seven. So your first guests might struggle a little.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: OK, I'll tell people not to come too early. Now, music. My cousin's band is playing. Is that all right?

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Of course. Our licence runs until midnight on Saturdays. It's only on weekday evenings that things have to stop at eleven.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: And would they have to use your sound system?

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: No, they don't need to, most bands prefer their own. What we do ask, though, is that you put a short note through the doors of the houses on Mill Lane, at least a week before the party, so they know there'll be some noise. We've had complaints in the past when people weren't warned.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That's fair enough. I can do that.

items.title: Open Day at Brickfield City Farm
items.context: A volunteer coordinator briefs a group of new volunteers before a city farm's open day.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking to a group of new volunteers about a city farm's open day. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Right, good morning, everyone, and thank you so much for coming along. I'm Megan, I coordinate the volunteers here at Brickfield City Farm, and I'll be your main point of contact on Saturday. I know one or two of you have helped out before, but most of you are new, so I'll go through everything from the beginning.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Now, you may have heard that this is our twentieth year, and yes, there will be a cake. A very large one. But the anniversary isn't really why we're holding the open day. Nor is it mainly about money. We'll have collection buckets, of course, but the new roof for the goat barn has already been paid for by a council grant.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: The honest truth is that we're seriously short of regular helpers, especially on weekday mornings, and an open day is far and away the best way we've found of signing people up. So if anyone shows an interest, please send them to the green gazebo.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: A few things are different from last year. Last time, we charged visitors three pounds at the gate, which caused long queues and, frankly, put some local families off. This year, thanks to a sponsor, there won't be any charge at all. Some people have rung up asking whether they need to book a place online. They don't, they can just turn up. And the hours are exactly the same as before: ten until four.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Right, the animals. The rabbits are always the most popular, with the guinea pigs a close second. Children can feed them, we sell little bags of feed for fifty pence, and that's absolutely fine.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: What we don't allow is children walking around holding them. Rabbits wriggle, and if they're dropped they can be badly hurt. So the rule is that the child sits down on the bench first, and then you place the rabbit on a towel on their lap. Last year we put the rabbits back in their hutches at lunchtime to give them a rest, but in fact they coped perfectly well, so they'll be out all day this time.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: People often ask me what I worry about most on the day. Parking always looks chaotic from the gate, but it does sort itself out, because the school next door lets us use their playground. And the queue for the café can get long, but people are usually very patient when there's cake involved.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: No, what really keeps me awake is the lost children's point. Last year we had eleven children separated from their parents in a single afternoon, and one little boy was missing for nearly forty minutes. So whoever's on that point needs to stay there, and not wander off to help elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: And the weather. If it rains, the tractor rides will still run, because the trailer's covered. We used to move the craft tables into the big barn when it rained, but the noise upset the animals, so now they go into the classroom instead. The only activity we'll actually call off is the pony rides. The ground gets far too slippery.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: OK, if you look at the plan I've given you, I'll show you where everything's going to be on the day. We're standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan, facing into the farm, so north is straight ahead. The main path runs from here up to the duck pond in the middle. It then splits and goes round both sides of the pond, and the two halves join up again on the far side.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: First aid. In previous years the first-aid post was right beside the café, which is just inside the gate on your left. But it got far too crowded there, so this year it's moving further up on the same side, right against the west fence, just south of the big barn. So it isn't on the main path at all. It's over by the fence.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Now, the lost children's point, and please do remember where this is. Lots of parents assume it'll be at the entrance, and we'll put a sign up here, but the point itself is beyond the pond, at the place where the two paths meet again. So that's on the north side of the pond.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Pony rides. You'd expect them to be in the paddock, but the paddock's being used for the sheep-shearing display this year. So the ponies will be in the small field in the bottom right-hand corner of the site, the south-east corner, to your right as you come in.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: The plant sale is new this year. It'll be along the north fence, at the very top of the plan, halfway between the big barn and the orchard. It won't be inside the orchard itself, I'm afraid, because the trees are being pruned that week.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: And finally, the cheese-making demonstration. Originally we'd planned to have it in the barn, by the door, but there just isn't enough light in there. So it'll be over on the east side of the site, between the orchard and the paddock, right up against the east fence.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Right, that's everything from me. Grab a coffee, and I'll come round and give you your T-shirts.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

items.title: Dissertation: Food-Packaging Waste in Supermarkets
items.context: Two students, Kirsty and Owen, discuss their joint dissertation on food-packaging waste in supermarkets with their tutor, Dr Lawson.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Kirsty and Owen, talking to their tutor about their dissertation on food-packaging waste in supermarkets. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson
transcript.text: Come in, both of you, have a seat. So, it's been about a month since we last met. How's the packaging project going?

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Pretty well, I think. Though you'll have noticed from the outline that it's changed quite a bit since then.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson
transcript.text: Yes, I did. You were originally going to look at plastic waste across the whole retail sector, weren't you? Now it's just food packaging in supermarkets. Was that because of what I said about the scope?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Well, you did say it was ambitious, and to be fair you were right. But honestly, we'd probably have stuck with it if we could. The real problem was that the council wouldn't give us the waste figures broken down by type of business. They said the data simply wasn't held in that form.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Whereas the supermarkets publish their own packaging reports, so at least there's something to work with.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson
transcript.text: And there I was thinking you'd taken my advice. Still, it's a much tighter project now, and a great deal more manageable. So, you've done your store visits now?

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Yeah, three stores, all in the city centre. And some of it wasn't what we expected at all. We'd assumed loose fruit and veg would be dearer than the packaged stuff...

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Which it was, in one shop.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: In one shop, sure, but in the other two it actually worked out cheaper per kilo. What really struck us was how little room it got. In the biggest store the loose produce took up barely a fifth of the display.

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: And the managers kept telling us that loose items get bruised and damaged more, so there's more waste. But honestly, we didn't see much sign of that.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson
transcript.text: Interesting. Let's talk about your shopper survey. How many responses have you got?

transcript.speaker: Owen
transcript.text: Sixty-two. We know that's not huge.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson
transcript.text: For a dissertation, that's perfectly defensible, I wouldn't worry about the numbers. And I know some people would say you should have done it online rather than standing outside shops with clipboards, but face to face tends to get you more thoughtful answers.

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson
transcript.text: No, my concern is the wording. Take question four. You ask people whether they agree that supermarkets use far too much unnecessary plastic. You're more or less telling people what to think.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Yeah... reading it back, it's not exactly neutral, is it?

transcript.speaker: Dr Lawson

items.title: The History and Science of Glassmaking
items.context: A lecturer gives a talk on what glass is and how glassmaking developed from the ancient world to the present.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the history and science of glassmaking. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a material that's so familiar we hardly notice it: glass. I want to look first at what glass actually is, and then trace how people learned to make it, and to make it better, over roughly four and a half thousand years.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, the science. Most of the solids we think of as hard, metals, salt, ice, are crystalline. Their atoms are lined up in a neat, repeating lattice, rather like soldiers on parade. Glass isn't like that. When you examine its structure, the arrangement of the atoms is random. It's essentially the structure of a liquid that's been frozen in place before it had time to organise itself.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This has given rise to a famous myth, which I'm sure some of you have heard: that glass is really a very slow-moving liquid, and that's why old church windows are thicker at the bottom. It isn't true. Calculations suggest that glass at room temperature wouldn't flow noticeably in the entire lifetime of the universe. The thick bottoms are simply because glaziers tended to put the heavier edge of an uneven pane at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The main ingredient of most glass is silica, which in practice means sand. The difficulty is that pure silica only melts at around seventeen hundred degrees Celsius, far hotter than any ancient furnace could reach. So glassmakers added soda, that is, sodium carbonate, which brings the melting point down dramatically. An ingredient that does this job is known as a flux, and do note that word, because you'll meet it again and again in the literature.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But soda on its own creates a problem. Soda glass is chemically unstable. Strange as it sounds, it will slowly dissolve in water. People often guess that it's acid that attacks it, but in fact ordinary rain is quite enough, given time. The solution was to add lime, which acts as a stabiliser, and that combination of sand, soda and lime is still the basis of about ninety per cent of the glass made today.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now to the history. The oldest glass objects we know of come from Mesopotamia, from about four and a half thousand years ago. You might imagine cups or bottles, but those didn't appear for another thousand years or so. The earliest objects were beads: small, brightly coloured, and treated almost like precious stones.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The real revolution came in the first century BC, probably somewhere along the coast of what's now Syria, with the invention of glassblowing. Instead of slowly shaping glass around a core, a worker could gather molten glass on the end of a hollow tube and blow it into shape in a matter of seconds. Suddenly, glass was cheap.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The Romans adopted the technique with great enthusiasm. They did make some window glass, though it was thick and not very transparent. But the commonest use for blown glass was containers. Now, you might expect these held wine. In fact wine was mostly kept in clay jars called amphorae, which were cheaper and far less fragile. Glass was particularly valued for perfume, because unlike clay, it doesn't absorb the scent or alter it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's jump forward to medieval Venice, which became the centre of European glassmaking. In twelve ninety-one the city ordered all its glassmakers to move to the nearby island of Murano. You'll often read that this was done to protect trade secrets, and it certainly helped with that. But the official reason given in the decree was the danger of fire. Venice was a crowded city full of wooden buildings, and the furnaces burned day and night.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Murano's great achievement was a glass called cristallo, which was almost colourless. Ordinary glass had a greenish tint, which comes from iron in the sand. It isn't caused by copper, as is sometimes claimed; copper tends to give a blue colour. The Venetians found that adding a small amount of manganese cancelled out the green, which is why manganese is sometimes nicknamed glassmaker's soap.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In England, in the sixteen seventies, George Ravenscroft began adding lead oxide to his glass. People assume lead glass must be stronger, but it's actually rather softer, which makes it easier to cut. What it gained was brilliance. Lead makes glass bend light much more, so when it's cut into facets, it sparkles. That's the origin of what we call lead crystal, which, ironically, given what I said earlier, isn't a crystal at all.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For centuries, making flat glass for windows remained difficult. You either blew a large cylinder and cut it open, or spun a disc. Both methods left the glass slightly wavy and uneven. The breakthrough came in the nineteen fifties with the float process, developed by Alastair Pilkington in Britain.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the float process, molten glass is poured continuously onto a bath of molten tin. People sometimes assume mercury was used, because it's liquid at room temperature, but it boils far too easily. Tin stays liquid over the whole working range, and because its surface is perfectly flat, the glass floating on top ends up perfectly flat as well. Almost all window glass is made this way today.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, a word about safety glass. Toughened glass is made by heating ordinary glass and then cooling the outside very quickly using jets of air. Water was tried, but it cools the surface so violently that the glass simply cracks. This rapid cooling puts the surface under compression, which makes the glass several times stronger. And if it does break, it shatters into small, blunt pieces rather than dangerous shards.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next week we'll look at more modern uses, glass in fibre-optic cables and so on, so please read chapter six before then.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.

items.title: Joining a Car-Share Club
items.context: A woman phones a city car-share club to become a member.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a car-share club to become a member. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 7.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Harbour Car Share, Craig speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, hi, Craig. I'd like to join the club, please. The online form kept freezing on me, so I thought I'd just ring.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Yeah, sorry about that. No worries, I can do it over the phone. Can I start with your name?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Sure. It's Joanna Pellowe.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: And how do you spell the surname?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: P... E... double L... O... W... E.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: P... E... double L... O... W...

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Sorry, there's an E on the end as well. People always leave it off.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Got it, with the E. And your home address?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: It's flat six, forty-two Lennox Street, in Rozelle.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Lennox Street... and the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Two-oh-three-nine... no, hang on, that's the office. Home is two-oh-three-seven.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Two-oh-three-seven. Lovely. Now, we ask everyone what they'll mainly be using the cars for. Is it mostly for work, or...?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Not for work, no. I cycle to the office. I used to borrow a friend's car to take my sister to the airport, but she's moved to Perth now, so... these days it'd mostly be to drive up and see my grandmother. She lives in a little town in the Blue Mountains, and the train doesn't go all the way.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Yeah, the trains up there aren't great at weekends. And which of our car bays would be handiest for you? In Rozelle we've got three.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Well, the one at the light rail stop would be ideal, but every time I've looked on the map, the cars there are booked out. Craig: That one's very popular, I'm afraid.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: And the bay outside the library, I thought that'd be the closest, but...

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Ah, that one's actually closed till the end of the year. The council's digging up the road there.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Right, then put me down for the one behind the swimming pool. It's only a five-minute walk, so that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Behind the pool, no problem. You can change that any time in the app anyway. Now, we've got three plans. There's Casual, which has no monthly fee but higher hourly rates; there's Plus, which has a small monthly fee and cheaper hours; and Premium, which is really for people who drive most days.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: I was thinking Casual, because I honestly won't drive that much. Maybe twice a month?

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: You could. But two return trips to the mountains a month, they're long bookings, say six or seven hours each. On Casual you'd be paying the higher rate the whole time. I reckon the middle one would work out cheaper for you.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Hmm... yeah, if they're full-day trips... Okay, you've talked me into it. I'll go for Plus. Not Premium, though, that's way more than I need.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Fair enough. Plus it is.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: And what's the monthly fee on that? The website said twelve dollars fifty.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Ah, that's last year's figure, the page hasn't been updated. It went up in July. It's fourteen dollars ninety-five a month now.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Fourteen ninety-five. Okay. Still a lot cheaper than running my own car.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Definitely. Now, we'll need a scan of your driver's licence, front and back, and something showing your address. A bank statement's fine...

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: I don't get paper statements any more. It's all online, and the screenshots don't actually show my address.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Right. We used to take mobile phone bills, but we can't accept those any more, head office changed the rules. Have you got a gas or an electricity bill?

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: The gas is in my flatmate's name, but I can send you my electricity bill, that's got my name and address on it.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Perfect. Just email it to us with the licence scan.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 8 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Can I ask about the rules? What happens if I'm late bringing a car back? The traffic coming down from the mountains can be awful on a Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: It happens. If you can, extend the booking in the app before it runs out. If you don't, there is a charge. It used to be a flat twenty-five dollars, whatever happened, which people thought was a bit harsh if they were only five minutes over.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: I can imagine.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: So now it's worked out in blocks of fifteen minutes. You pay a small fee for each block you're over. We don't charge you for a whole extra hour, which is what some of the other clubs do.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: That sounds fairer. And is there anything I have to do before I drive off? Do I need to ring you?

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: You don't need to call us. That's what we used to ask, but the app does all that now. Some members check the petrol gauge, but honestly, our staff refuel the cars, and there's a fuel card in the glovebox if you do run low, so that's not something you need to worry about.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, right. Craig: The one thing we do insist on is that you walk around the car and take pictures of any scratches or dents in the app. Otherwise you could end up getting blamed for them.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Good to know. I'll make sure I do that.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: So, would you like to make your first booking now? Your membership card takes about five days to come in the post.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, so I'd have to wait for that anyway?

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: No, no, you don't need the card. Once your documents are approved, you can unlock the cars with your phone. That's usually the same day.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Oh, good. I was hoping to go up this Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: Let me see... yep, the hatchback behind the pool is free all day Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Actually... I'd better not book it yet. My grandmother sometimes goes to her bridge club on a Saturday, and I don't want to drive all that way if she isn't going to be home. I'll ring her tonight and then book it in the app.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: No problem at all. I'll email you a link to the app in the next few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Joanna
transcript.text: Great. Thanks so much for your help, Craig.

transcript.speaker: Craig
transcript.text: My pleasure, Joanna. Enjoy the drive.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

items.title: The Ashcombe Heritage Trail
items.context: A local radio presenter introduces the council's heritage officer, who describes a new heritage trail in the town.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear a local radio presenter introducing a heritage officer, who is talking about a new heritage trail in her town. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 16.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Good morning, and welcome back to Ashcombe Today. Now, those small metal discs that have appeared in the town centre pavements are part of the new Ashcombe Heritage Trail, which opens this Saturday, and here to tell us all about it is the council's heritage officer, Ruth Penhale. Morning, Ruth.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Morning, Steve, and thanks for having me. Well, the trail links fourteen places of interest in the old town, but this morning I'll just pick out six of the main ones.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Let's start at the Corn Exchange on the High Street. A lot of people still think of it as the place to get a coffee, and there was a café on the ground floor for years, but it closed last spring and the space is empty for now. What you will find just inside the entrance hall is a model of the town as it looked in about eighteen fifty. It was built by pupils from Ashcombe Primary as a class project last term, and it's remarkably detailed. They even put tiny sheep in the market square.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: From there, the trail goes down Well Lane to St Bride's Well. This is one of the oldest sites in the town; there's been a spring there since medieval times. We'd originally planned to put one of our audio posts there, where you press a button and hear a short recording, but the budget didn't stretch that far, sadly.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: And I should warn listeners: the well sits at the bottom of a flight of very narrow, uneven steps. We did look into putting in a ramp, but because the stonework is protected, we weren't given permission. So I'm afraid it isn't a stop that anyone in a wheelchair will be able to get down to.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Just past the well, you come to the Tannery Bridge over the river. Now, generations of Ashcombe people have called it the black bridge, because that's the colour it's been for as long as anyone can remember. But when our conservation team scraped back the layers of paint last year, they discovered the ironwork had first been painted a deep green, and that's the shade you'll see there now. It's caused a few complaints, actually. Ruth: Then it's back up the hill to the Market Cross. You'll see people climbing the steps around the base hoping for a view, but to be honest, you can't see much from there; the buildings are too close. What makes the cross special is the bell at the top. The original was stolen in the nineteen seventies and never recovered. The one hanging there now was cast last year by a foundry in Devon, copied exactly from old photographs.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Round the corner from the cross are the Weavers' Cottages, a row of five little houses where cloth used to be made by hand. People are often disappointed to learn that they're all private homes now, so you can't just wander in. But the owners of the end cottage have very kindly agreed to let us in once a month, which means the only way to see inside is to book a place on one of our guided walks.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: And finally, there's the old Railway Goods Shed, down by the station car park. There's one of our audio posts inside, and if you press the button, you'll hear recordings we made with men and women who worked on the railway in the nineteen fifties and sixties.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: A lot of people ask me whether there's somewhere to eat in the shed. There isn't, I'm afraid, though the Signal Box Café is just over the road. And if you're after a view over the whole town, the best place is really the old water tower behind the station, but that's not part of the trail, because it isn't open to the public.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 17 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Ruth, tell us about those discs in the pavement.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Ah, the markers. Well, there was quite a debate about those. Some councillors wanted them made from recycled plastic, to be environmentally friendly, but in the end we went for bronze, because it lasts so much longer. They were designed by Ellen Marsh, a sculptor who's lived in Ashcombe all her life. They shouldn't need replacing for a very long time; we're hoping they'll still be there in fifty years.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: As for how long it takes, the leaflet says forty-five minutes, but that's if you walk briskly and don't stop at all. If you actually read the information boards, I'd allow about an hour and a half. Some people make a whole morning of it and have lunch at the end, but that's up to you.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: There's also a free app to go with the trail. Some people tell me they prefer it to the printed leaflet, but personally I find the map in the leaflet much easier to follow. There's a paid version of the app with extra content, too, but honestly, the free one has everything most visitors would need.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: My main piece of advice is this: the mobile signal in the old streets is terrible. So if you want to use the app, make sure you've got it on your phone before you leave home.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: And is there any way listeners can get involved?

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Well, we've had a wonderful response to our appeal for volunteer guides. In fact, we've got all the guides we need for this year, so thank you to everyone who came forward. Last year we asked people to suggest buildings to include, and that went well, too.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: What we're short of now is pictures. If you've got old photographs of the town in a drawer at home, shops, street parties, anything, we'd love to scan them for the trail website. You can drop them at the library, and we'll return them within a week.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Lovely. Ruth Penhale, thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

items.title: Seminar Presentation: How Young Children Acquire Language
items.context: Two students, Hannah and Liam, prepare a seminar presentation on how young children acquire language.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Hannah and Liam, preparing a seminar presentation on how young children acquire language. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 24.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Okay, Liam, we've got twenty minutes for the whole presentation, including questions, so we really need to decide what goes in and what comes out.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah, fair enough. I made a list last night. Shall we go through it?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Go on.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Right, first, Chomsky, and the idea that we're born with some kind of built-in grammar.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Hmm. I mean, it's important, obviously, but everyone in the group did that to death in first year. If we spend five minutes on it, people will just switch off.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: True. So we cut it, then. We can mention his name in passing, but not give it a section. Next, kids who grow up with two languages.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I was wondering about dropping that, actually. It's such a huge area.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Ah, no, I really think we need it. Half the people in our seminar group grew up speaking more than one language at home. They'll want to hear about it.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Fair point. Keep it, but keep it short. What's next?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Children learning sign language. There's that brilliant study from Nicaragua.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd love to include that, but realistically, we'd have to explain how sign languages work first, and we just haven't got the time.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah, you're right. It'd need a whole presentation of its own. And what about screen time, whether toddlers pick up words from the television?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd have said drop that, to be honest. The research is pretty thin.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: But that's kind of the point, isn't it? Everyone assumes educational programmes help, and the evidence says they mostly don't, not unless an adult is watching and talking about it with the child. That's a nice surprising finding. Just a minute or two. Hannah: All right, you win. And then babbling, which obviously stays. It's where everything starts.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Definitely.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Okay. Then the main section: child-directed speech. You know, the way adults talk to babies, with the high pitch and the exaggerated tune. Did anything in the reading surprise you?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: A couple of things. I'd always assumed it was mainly mothers who did it, and that dads sort of talked to babies the same way they talk to anyone else. But that study showed fathers change their voices just as much. That really surprised me.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Mm. What about the bit showing that newborns would rather listen to it than to normal adult speech? I thought that was amazing, at only a few days old.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Honestly, that didn't really surprise me. Babies like anything that sounds a bit musical. What did get me was that it isn't universal. I'd taken it for granted that every culture does it, but there are communities where adults hardly speak directly to babies at all, and the kids still learn to talk perfectly well.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Yes, that was striking. And older brothers and sisters doing it to toddlers, I found that quite unexpected.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Not me. I've got a four-year-old niece, and she talks to her baby brother exactly like that.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Fair enough. And the old claim that it holds back vocabulary?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Well, nobody really believes that any more. The studies show the opposite, which is pretty much what I'd have expected.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 25 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Now, about the video. I was planning to show that clip of my cousin's little boy, the one where he's naming everything in the garden.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: It's lovely, but it's nearly ten minutes long, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Oh, I'd only play a minute of it, I can cut it down easily. And the sound's fine, I recorded it on a decent microphone. But I've decided not to use it after all. I mentioned it to my cousin, and she wasn't keen on her son being shown to a room full of strangers.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: No, absolutely, that's her call. We'll find something online instead.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Then I want to do the 'wug' experiment. You know, the one where kids are shown a drawing of a made-up creature called a wug, and then two of them, and they have to finish the sentence: 'There are two...'

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Isn't it a bit old, though? It was done in the nineteen fifties.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: It's old, but it hasn't dated at all. I don't think there's anything that shows more clearly that kids aren't just copying what they hear. They've never heard the word 'wugs', so they must be applying a rule.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Some people say the results were overstated, though. That a lot of the kids were just guessing.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I've read that critique, and I don't buy it. The results have been repeated loads of times.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Okay. That leads nicely into mistakes like 'I goed' or 'two mouses'.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah. Parents get really worried about those.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And they correct them constantly, which, according to everything we read, makes almost no difference.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Right. And people think they've stopped by about four, but actually some kids carry on making them till they're six or seven. Hannah: The point we need to get across is that they're not a sign that anything's wrong. It's the reverse, really: the child has worked out the rule and is just using it too widely. That's a step forward.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Agreed. That's our key message for that section.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: What about a handout? Last time the tutor said ours was far too long.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'd rather not give anything out at the start. People just read it instead of listening.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: We could put all the references on the final slide...

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Nobody can copy down twenty references in the thirty seconds it's up.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Okay, so let's email a one-page summary to everyone once the session's over.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Yes, that's the best option.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I'm a bit worried about questions at the end, though. What if someone asks something we can't answer?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: That doesn't bother me. We just say we'll look into it. And we've left five minutes, which is plenty. What I'm more concerned about is what happened last term, when we asked for questions and there was total silence. It was so awkward.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Oh, I remember. So should we get a friend to ask something?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Better than that, we'll finish with a question for them to discuss in pairs. That'll get them talking.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Right. So what next? Should we book a meeting with Dr Morgan to check the plan?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I don't think we need to. She said she's happy as long as we stick to the outline. And we can't really run through it properly till the slides are finished.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: True. The problem is, most of our sources are from the nineties. We need some recent research, especially on bilingualism.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Okay, let's both spend tomorrow in the library looking for studies from the last five years, and then meet up again on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

items.title: Urban Heat Islands
items.context: A lecturer in urban geography gives a talk on the causes and effects of urban heat islands and on ways of reducing them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Okay, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a topic that's become increasingly urgent for city planners, and that's what's known as the urban heat island: the simple fact that cities are often a great deal hotter than the countryside around them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The difference can be dramatic. In extreme cases, a large city can be as much as twelve degrees warmer than the farmland that surrounds it. And here's what surprises most people. The gap isn't at its greatest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun is strongest. It's widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it has soaked up during the day for hours after sunset, while the countryside cools down quite quickly.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what causes it? Well, the first factor is the materials we build with. Dark surfaces like asphalt and roofing tar absorb most of the sunlight that hits them, rather than bouncing it back. Scientists describe this property using the term albedo, that's A... L... B... E... D... O, which is simply a measure of how much light a surface reflects.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Fresh snow, for example, has a very high albedo; it sends most of the light back into the sky. Asphalt, on the other hand, has an extremely low albedo, which is why a parking lot in July can burn your feet.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second factor is the shape of the city. Tall buildings placed close together form what are called urban canyons. Heat bounces back and forth between the walls and gets trapped, and the buildings also block the wind that would otherwise carry that warm air away.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And third, there's what we call waste heat: the heat given off by human activity. You'd probably guess that traffic is the main source, and in a lot of cities, that's true. But in the case study I'll be referring to throughout today, which looked at a mid-sized city in Ontario, it wasn't vehicles that produced the most waste heat. It was industry, largely because of a cluster of factories right next to downtown. Air conditioning units came a fairly distant third.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, the effects. The most obvious one is on health. Heat waves kill more people in North America each year than any other type of weather event, and the elderly are especially at risk, because the body's ability to cool itself declines with age.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But there's an economic side, too. When a city heats up, demand for electricity rises sharply, mainly because of all those air conditioners running at once, and utilities sometimes struggle to keep up. Natural gas use, by contrast, hardly changes at all in summer, so that isn't really where the costs come from.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also an effect on water that's often overlooked. When rain falls on hot pavement and rooftops, the water warms up before it drains into streams and rivers. And that's a real problem for fish that depend on cold water. In the Ontario study, researchers recorded a sharp decline in trout in the streams below the city. Not salmon, interestingly; they'd disappeared from that river long before the city expanded, so it's trout that are now under pressure.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, what can be done? Let's look at four approaches. The first is the cool roof. People tend to picture white roof tiles, but in fact most cool roofs are just ordinary roofs with a reflective coating applied on top, usually white or pale grey. It's cheap, it can go onto an existing building, and it can lower the surface temperature of a roof by thirty degrees or more.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second approach is the green roof, a roof planted with vegetation. Green roofs cool the air through evaporation, and they soak up rainwater, which helps reduce flooding. They're a lot more expensive than cool roofs, though, and many older buildings simply aren't strong enough to support the weight of wet soil.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The third approach, and probably the one residents like best, is planting street trees. But not all trees are equally useful. The key thing isn't how tall a tree grows. What really matters is having wide canopies, that's the spreading layer of branches and leaves that actually throws shade onto the street. A tall, narrow tree like a poplar does surprisingly little.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the Ontario city, the tree-planting program was interesting because of where it was targeted. You might expect planners to start with the oldest neighbourhoods, or with the downtown core, where it's hottest. Instead, they focused on districts where people had a low income, because those areas had the fewest trees to begin with, and residents there were the least likely to own air conditioners.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The fourth approach is the cool pavement: road and sidewalk surfaces that are made lighter in colour. These do work, but they've turned out to have an unexpected drawback. On bright days, the light reflected off them creates glare, which pedestrians find really uncomfortable, and some studies suggest they can actually make people walking on them feel hotter, not cooler.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So why haven't these measures been adopted everywhere? You'd assume the main obstacle is the initial cost, and that's certainly an issue. data.title: Urban Heat Islands
data.context: A lecturer in urban geography gives a talk on the causes and effects of urban heat islands and on ways of reducing them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Okay, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're turning to a topic that's become increasingly urgent for city planners, and that's what's known as the urban heat island: the simple fact that cities are often a great deal hotter than the countryside around them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The difference can be dramatic. In extreme cases, a large city can be as much as twelve degrees warmer than the farmland that surrounds it. And here's what surprises most people. The gap isn't at its greatest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun is strongest. It's widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it has soaked up during the day for hours after sunset, while the countryside cools down quite quickly.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what causes it? Well, the first factor is the materials we build with. Dark surfaces like asphalt and roofing tar absorb most of the sunlight that hits them, rather than bouncing it back. Scientists describe this property using the term albedo, that's A... L... B... E... D... O, which is simply a measure of how much light a surface reflects.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Fresh snow, for example, has a very high albedo; it sends most of the light back into the sky. Asphalt, on the other hand, has an extremely low albedo, which is why a parking lot in July can burn your feet.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second factor is the shape of the city. Tall buildings placed close together form what are called urban canyons. Heat bounces back and forth between the walls and gets trapped, and the buildings also block the wind that would otherwise carry that warm air away.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And third, there's what we call waste heat: the heat given off by human activity. You'd probably guess that traffic is the main source, and in a lot of cities, that's true. But in the case study I'll be referring to throughout today, which looked at a mid-sized city in Ontario, it wasn't vehicles that produced the most waste heat. It was industry, largely because of a cluster of factories right next to downtown. Air conditioning units came a fairly distant third.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, the effects. The most obvious one is on health. Heat waves kill more people in North America each year than any other type of weather event, and the elderly are especially at risk, because the body's ability to cool itself declines with age.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But there's an economic side, too. When a city heats up, demand for electricity rises sharply, mainly because of all those air conditioners running at once, and utilities sometimes struggle to keep up. Natural gas use, by contrast, hardly changes at all in summer, so that isn't really where the costs come from.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also an effect on water that's often overlooked. When rain falls on hot pavement and rooftops, the water warms up before it drains into streams and rivers. And that's a real problem for fish that depend on cold water. In the Ontario study, researchers recorded a sharp decline in trout in the streams below the city. Not salmon, interestingly; they'd disappeared from that river long before the city expanded, so it's trout that are now under pressure.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, what can be done? Let's look at four approaches. The first is the cool roof. People tend to picture white roof tiles, but in fact most cool roofs are just ordinary roofs with a reflective coating applied on top, usually white or pale grey. It's cheap, it can go onto an existing building, and it can lower the surface temperature of a roof by thirty degrees or more.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second approach is the green roof, a roof planted with vegetation. Green roofs cool the air through evaporation, and they soak up rainwater, which helps reduce flooding. They're a lot more expensive than cool roofs, though, and many older buildings simply aren't strong enough to support the weight of wet soil.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The third approach, and probably the one residents like best, is planting street trees. But not all trees are equally useful. The key thing isn't how tall a tree grows. What really matters is having wide canopies, that's the spreading layer of branches and leaves that actually throws shade onto the street. A tall, narrow tree like a poplar does surprisingly little.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In the Ontario city, the tree-planting program was interesting because of where it was targeted. You might expect planners to start with the oldest neighbourhoods, or with the downtown core, where it's hottest. Instead, they focused on districts where people had a low income, because those areas had the fewest trees to begin with, and residents there were the least likely to own air conditioners.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The fourth approach is the cool pavement: road and sidewalk surfaces that are made lighter in colour. These do work, but they've turned out to have an unexpected drawback. On bright days, the light reflected off them creates glare, which pedestrians find really uncomfortable, and some studies suggest they can actually make people walking on them feel hotter, not cooler.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So why haven't these measures been adopted everywhere? You'd assume the main obstacle is the initial cost, and that's certainly an issue. But the city officials interviewed in the Ontario study said that wasn't really what held them back. The bigger problem, they said, was maintenance. Reflective coatings get dirty and gradually lose their effect, and young trees need regular watering for several years. The money for that kind of upkeep just isn't there in most budgets.

items.title: Booking a Canal Narrowboat Holiday
items.context: A man phones a holiday company to book a week on a canal narrowboat for his family.

speakers.name: Lorna
speakers.role: Booking adviser at a canal holiday company

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a holiday company to book a canal narrowboat holiday. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 1 to 5.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Good morning, Hartwell Waterways, Lorna speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Oh, hello. I'm hoping to book a narrowboat for a week this summer. I've never done anything like this before, so, er, bear with me.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Not at all, most of our customers are first-timers. Let me just take a few details first. Could I have your name?

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Yes, it's Martin Wardrop.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Is that spelt like the furniture? W-A-R-D-R-O-B-E?

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Everybody says that. No, it's W... A... R... D... R... O... P. There's no E on the end.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: W... A... R... D... R... O... P. Lovely. And how many of you will be on the boat?

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Well, it was going to be six. My sister and her husband were coming, but they've had to pull out because of work. So it's just me, my wife and our two boys now.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: So that's four of you altogether, then.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: And how old are the boys? We put life jackets on board, so I need to know which sizes to give you.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Nine and twelve. Well, the younger one's nine now, but he'll be ten by August.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Two junior sizes, then. And they'll need to wear them on deck at all times, I'm afraid, even if they're strong swimmers.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: They won't like that, but fair enough.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: And when were you thinking of going? Our hire weeks run Saturday to Saturday.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Some time in August. We'd set off on Saturday the twenty-third, I think... no, hang on, that's the day we'd have to be home. So we'd set off on the sixteenth.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Departing the sixteenth of August, back on the twenty-third. Yes, I've got boats available that week. Now, which of our bases would suit you? There are three on this stretch of the canal.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: The website mentioned Stoke Lock. That's the nearest one to us.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: I'm afraid Stoke Lock is fully booked for the whole of August. And Abbey Basin isn't really an option either, because the canal's closed there until September while they replace the lock gates. But we do have boats at Orchard Wharf, which is only about twenty minutes further on.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Orchard Wharf. That's fine, we're driving anyway.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Speaking of which, you can leave your car at the wharf while you're away. It's twelve pounds a day...

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Twelve a day? So that'd be, er, eighty-four for the week?

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: No, no. If you pay for the whole week up front, it's a flat rate of forty-five pounds. It used to be free, but the landowner started charging last year.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Forty-five. That's not bad at all. Er, one other thing that worries me. Do we need any experience? I've only ever rowed a dinghy on a boating lake.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: You'd be surprised how many people say that. No experience needed. Before you leave, one of our staff spends about an hour on the boat with you, showing you how to steer and work the locks. Right, shall I tell you about the boats that are free that week?

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Yes, please.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 6 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: OK, there are three. The first is Kingfisher. She sleeps four, and she's the shortest of the three, which makes her much easier to handle. We often recommend her to beginners.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: That sounds ideal, actually.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: The one thing people do comment on is the space. The bedroom's fine, it's got a proper double bed, and the kitchen's very well equipped, but the shower is really tiny. If you're tall, you'll notice.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: I'm six foot two, so... noted. And what does she cost?

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: In June she'd be nine hundred and eighty pounds, but August is peak season, so for your week it's one thousand, one hundred and sixty.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: One thousand one hundred and sixty. OK.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: The second is Moorhen, which sleeps six, so you'd all have more room to spread out. We used to provide a couple of kayaks with her, but there were rather too many, er, accidents, so these days she comes with two bicycles instead. They're handy for riding along the towpath to the village shops.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Oh, the boys would love that. Is there a catch?

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: She's one of our older boats. I wouldn't say the engine's unreliable, because it was fully serviced in the spring, but it is quite loud, so whoever's steering at the back will hear it all day.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Fair enough. And the price for Moorhen?

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: One thousand, three hundred and twenty-five for the week.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: And the third is Heron, our newest boat. She was only launched in March, and she also sleeps six. People tend to assume she's got a washing machine, which she hasn't, but she does have a dishwasher, and that always goes down well.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: My wife would be thrilled. What's the downside?

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: She's the longest boat in the fleet, so she can't turn round in some of the narrower sections, and you'd have to plan your route much more carefully. She's one thousand, four hundred and ninety.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Hmm. I was leaning towards Kingfisher, but with my height... I think it'll be Moorhen. The bikes swing it, really.

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: Lovely, I'll reserve her for you now. We'll need a deposit of a quarter of the total within seven days, and I'll email you the paperwork this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Brilliant. Can I pay the deposit by card over the phone?

transcript.speaker: Lorna
transcript.text: You can, or by bank transfer if you prefer. The details are on the confirmation email. The balance is then due six weeks before you travel.

transcript.speaker: Martin
transcript.text: Card's easiest. Thanks so much for your help, Lorna.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

items.context: The front-of-house manager at a theatre gives an induction talk to a group of new volunteer ushers.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear the front-of-house manager at a theatre giving an induction talk to some new volunteer ushers. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 11 to 15.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: Right, good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Corran Theatre. I'm Diane, I run front of house, which means that for the next few months you'll be seeing rather a lot of me. Thank you all for volunteering.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: We'll start with a quick tour of the ground floor, because the first thing audiences do is ask you where things are. So, we're standing just inside the main entrance, facing into the building. The box office is right here on your right, and the bar runs along the whole of the left-hand wall.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: Now, the cloakroom. Regular visitors will tell you it's next to the box office, because that's where it used to be. It isn't any more; that space is now the shop, selling programmes and souvenirs. The cloakroom has moved to the opposite side, in the corner immediately to your left as you come through the doors, just before the bar begins.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: Straight ahead of us is the grand staircase, which takes you up to the circle, and on either side of it there's a set of double doors into the stalls. To the left of the staircase, a corridor runs all the way along the side of the auditorium, and there's a matching one on the right.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: Let's take the left-hand corridor first. The first door you come to, on your left, says Technical Store. That's not ours, please don't go in there. Keep walking right to the far end, and the door facing you is the volunteers' room. That's where you'll leave your bags, sign in and get your briefing before each show.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: People are always surprised by where we've put the lift. You'd expect it beside the main staircase, wouldn't you? But it isn't. It's tucked away in the alcove at the far end of the bar, in the back left-hand corner of the foyer, so if someone in a wheelchair asks, send them past the bar, not towards the stairs.

transcript.speaker: Diane
transcript.text: Now the right-hand corridor. About halfway along, on your right, is the first-aid room. Don't confuse it with the door at the very end of that corridor. That leads backstage to the stage door, and it's strictly for cast and crew.

transcript.speaker: Diane

items.title: River Erosion Field-Trip Report
items.context: Two geography students, Hannah and Callum, discuss the draft of their field-trip report on river bank erosion with their lecturer, Dr Mercer.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear two geography students, Hannah and Callum, talking to their lecturer, Dr Mercer, about their field-trip report on river erosion. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 21 to 25.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Come in, both of you, sit down. So, I've read your draft on the erosion fieldwork at Ashcombe. There's a lot of good material in it, but structurally it needs some work, so let's go through it section by section.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Great, thanks. We were a bit worried about the length, actually.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Rightly so. Let's start with the site description.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I did wonder if we could just cut that altogether. Everyone on the module knows the site. We all went there on the same day.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Your external examiner didn't, though. No, it needs to stay. But at the moment it's sitting on its own and repeating half of what's already in your introduction. I'd fold the two together into a single section.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: That makes sense. One tidy section rather than two half-empty ones.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Then the methods. Now, this is very thorough...

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Too thorough? Should we shorten it?

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: I wouldn't cut a word of it, actually. It's accurate, and someone could repeat your study from it. The trouble is that three pages on calibrating a flow meter interrupt the reader just when they want your argument. Keep a short summary in the main text, and put the step-by-step detail at the back, after the references.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Right, so the full procedure gets tucked in at the end as supplementary material.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Next, your velocity and discharge results. This is where I have real concerns. Your discharge figures are roughly a hundred times too big.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Aye, we wondered about that. Hannah thought the flow meter might've been faulty. Could we get one of the technicians to look at it?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I did think that at first, but...

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: There's nothing wrong with the meter. I've checked the log, and it was calibrated the day before you went out. The problem is that you measured the channel width in centimetres and the depth in metres and then multiplied them. So it's the working-out that has to be done again, from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Oh no. That's embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: It happens every year. Sediment analysis, now. The sieving results look plausible, but the weights for samples four, five and six are oddly identical, which makes me wonder whether the balance was misbehaving that day.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Could we add some close-up photos of the samples? Then people could see the difference in grain size for themselves.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Pictures won't tell anyone what anything weighs. Before you change a single number, take your raw data to Julia, the technician in the soils lab. She looks after the balances, and she'll tell you whether those readings can be trusted.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I'll email her today.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And should we wait to hear from her before we touch the discussion? Because if those weights change, our whole argument about grain size changes too.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Exactly. Don't rewrite anything that depends on those samples until she's had a look.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And the evaluation? We're well over the word limit, so I was thinking we could just drop it.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Absolutely not. It's a required section, and you'd lose marks. But it's currently longer than your results, which is the wrong way round. Bring it down to about half its present length, and focus on the two or three limitations that really matter.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: So halve it, don't bin it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 26 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Remind me why you chose that stretch of river. It's not the most obvious site.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Partly access. There's a footpath right down to the bank, so carrying all the kit was easy. But honestly, if that'd been the only thing, we'd have gone to the bridge site, which is even easier to get to.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: What actually decided it was that the department has records from exactly that stretch going back to the nineteen-nineties, so we could set our results against theirs. The meanders are lovely and pronounced as well, but that wasn't really why.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Good. Now, your erosion pins. You put twelve into the outer bank in March and measured them again in September.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We know twelve isn't many.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Actually, I don't think the number's the issue; twelve is perfectly respectable for a project this size. And you mention cattle possibly knocking them, but you said yourselves the field was fenced off. What worries me is that March to September misses the winter floods, and that's when most bank erosion takes place.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: Right. We hadn't thought of that.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Don't panic. You can't go back and measure in January now, but you must acknowledge it, and say what you'd expect a winter record to show.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Callum, how did you feel when you saw the outer bank figures?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Honestly? I'd expected the bank to have retreated by tens of centimetres, from everything in the textbooks, and it had hardly moved at all. It's not that I doubted the readings. We measured every pin twice. And they're nothing like the department's older figures either, which showed much faster retreat.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: So how are you going to explain that difference from the earlier data?

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: I think it's the stone wall the landowner built upstream about ten years ago. It's protecting the bank, so there's less energy reaching our site.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I'm not convinced. The wall's three hundred metres upstream. I'd say it's simply been a run of drier years, so there's been lower discharge.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: We've been going round in circles on that for a week.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Well, at least you agree on everything else. You're both happy with scatter graphs for the results?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Aye, no argument there.

transcript.speaker: Hannah
transcript.text: And we both want to keep the bits from our conversation with the farmer. That was really useful.

transcript.speaker: Dr Mercer
transcript.text: Then present both explanations and weigh them up. And before you submit... I'd normally suggest swapping drafts with another group, but nobody else worked on your stretch, so that won't help much. Your reference list is fine; don't touch it. What I'd like you to do is read Pearson's article on artificial bank protection. It'll give you the evidence to judge Hannah's theory properly.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Great. More reading. No, fair enough. Thanks, Dr Mercer.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.
