items.title: The Economics of the Medieval English Wool Trade
items.context: A lecturer in economic history gives a talk on the economics of the English wool trade in the Middle Ages.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the economics of the medieval English wool trade. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning. Today we're turning to what was, for several centuries, the backbone of the English economy: wool. One historian remarked that England in this period was little more than a sheep farm with a government attached. An exaggeration, certainly, but not a huge one.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So why was English wool so sought after? It wasn't a question of volume; later on, Spain produced considerably more. Nor was it the colour, which actually varied a good deal from region to region. What buyers in Flanders and Italy were paying for was its fineness, by which I mean how thin and soft the individual fibres were, because that determined the quality of the cloth they could weave.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, you might assume that the great flocks belonged to the aristocracy, to earls and barons with vast estates. Some did, of course. But the really large-scale producers were monasteries, particularly those of the Cistercian order, some of which kept ten or fifteen thousand sheep on the uplands of Yorkshire and the Welsh borders.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Wool was traded by the sack, a standard unit of about three hundred and sixty-four pounds in weight, or roughly the fleeces of two hundred and fifty sheep. At its peak, in the early fourteenth century, England was exporting somewhere in the region of thirty-five thousand sacks a year.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What's economically fascinating is how these monasteries sold their wool. Italian and Flemish merchants would pay for it in advance, sometimes for the next ten or even twenty years' production. Now, this wasn't strictly a loan, and it wasn't really investment in the modern sense either. Economic historians generally describe it as a form of credit: the abbeys were, in effect, borrowing against wool that hadn't yet grown.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And this was a risky arrangement. If an epidemic swept through a flock, an abbey could find itself owing years of wool that it simply couldn't deliver. The term contemporaries used for these outbreaks was murrain. That's M... U... double R... A... I... N. It was a rather vague word, covering almost any disease of cattle or sheep, and several abbeys were left heavily in debt by murrain in the late thirteenth century.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's turn now to the Crown, because English kings were very quick to see wool as a source of revenue. Export duties on wool became one of the largest items of royal income. It's often said that this money went into building castles, but in fact remarkably little did. Overwhelmingly, it paid for military campaigns, above all Edward the Third's campaigns in France during the Hundred Years' War.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To manage all this, the Crown created what was called the Staple: a single designated town through which all wool exports had to pass. The Staple moved around a great deal at first, between Bruges, Antwerp and a number of English ports, but from thirteen sixty-three it was fixed at Calais, then an English possession, and it remained there for almost two hundred years.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Officially, the Staple existed to guarantee quality, so that foreign buyers could trust what they were getting. That was the justification. But the real motive was far more practical. With all the wool passing through one place, collection of the tax became much simpler, and far harder to evade.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The merchants who ran the Staple became extremely wealthy, and they regularly lent money to the king, sometimes in return for reductions in the very duties they were supposed to be paying. So the relationship between the Crown and the wool merchants was, shall we say, rather cosy.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, these heavy duties on raw wool had an important side effect. Finished cloth was taxed much more lightly, so it increasingly made sense to weave the cloth in England and export that instead. And this shift was helped along by a change in a process called fulling. Fulling means beating woven cloth in water to thicken and clean it, and traditionally it was done by workers trampling it with their feet.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: By the fourteenth century, fulling was increasingly mechanised. Wind power was tried in some flatter areas, but it proved too unreliable. The mills that succeeded were driven by water, which is why the cloth industry gradually drifted away from the old towns towards hilly districts with fast-flowing streams, such as the Cotswolds and the Pennine valleys.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: You can still see the profits of all this today. Wealthy wool and cloth merchants spent lavishly on their parish churches, and the so-called wool churches of Suffolk and the Cotswolds are strikingly large for such small villages. If you visit, notice that it isn't spires that dominate; spires are actually quite rare in these areas. What you see are tall, elaborately decorated towers, often paid for by a single merchant family.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One more factor deserves a mention. After the Black Death in thirteen forty-eight, labour became scarce and expensive, and many landowners turned their fields over from crops to sheep, since a single shepherd could look after land that had once needed dozens of farm workers. That kept wool production high, even as exports of raw wool began to fall.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, decline. By the sixteenth century, English raw wool no longer dominated European markets. Partly that was because English weavers were now using so much of it themselves. But there was also serious competition from Spain, where a breed with an exceptionally fine fleece had been developed. Spanish merino wool gradually took over the luxury end of the market.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The legacy of the trade survives in some odd places. The Lord Speaker in the House of Lords still sits on the Woolsack, a large cushion stuffed with wool, as a reminder of where England's wealth once came from. Next week, we'll look at how the cloth industry developed in its own right.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.

items.title: Joining a Running Club
items.context: A man who has recently moved to Australia phones a running club about becoming a member and entering its charity ten-kilometre race.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Wattle Bay Runners, Jodie speaking.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Oh, hello. Um, I got this number from your website. I'm thinking about joining the club, and I was also hoping to find out about the ten-kilometre race you're organising.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Lovely, you've come to the right person. I'm the club secretary, so I can help you with both. Can I grab your name first?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Ben. Ben Thursby. I've only just moved here from Manchester, so I don't really know anyone yet.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Well, a running club's a great way to fix that. Have you been running long?

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: A few years, on and off. I did a couple of half marathons back home, but I've been a bit lazy since the move, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: No dramas. Right, so the club runs twice a week, Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and we start at six thirty.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: And where do you all meet? The website mentioned the library car park, I think.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Ah, yeah, sorry, the website's a bit out of date. We did use to meet at the library, but then the council started charging for parking there in the evenings. So these days we meet at the pavilion in Norfolk Park. It's the building right next to the cricket nets, you can't miss it.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The pavilion, next to the nets. Got it. And is there a membership fee?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: There is, it's an annual fee. It was sixty-five dollars last year, but we've had to put it up to seventy-two, mostly because our insurance went up.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Seventy-two. That's still very reasonable. Is there anything on top of that?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Only if you want a club singlet, and they're fifteen dollars. But that's entirely optional. Nobody makes you wear one to training.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Right... And what do I need to bring when I sign up? Do you need, um, a doctor's certificate or something? I know some clubs back in England ask for one.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: We used to, actually, but not any more. Now you just fill in a short health questionnaire on the night. What you will need to bring is a photo, because we print everyone a membership card, and the card gets you ten per cent off at the sports shop on the high street.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: A photo, fine, I can sort that out. Is there a group for people who are, er, getting back into it? I don't want to be left behind on my first night.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Everyone says that. Yes, there's a beginners' group on Tuesdays. It's run by one of our coaches, Gail Kerridge.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Sorry, was that Kerrigan?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: No, Kerridge. K... E... double R... I... D... G... E.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: K, E, double R, I, D, G, E. Thanks. And she always takes the beginners?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: She does now. She used to coach the juniors, but she swapped over this year, and honestly, she's brilliant with people who are nervous.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 5 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Now, the race. The charity ten K. When is it exactly? I saw a poster in a café that said the second of November.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Yeah, a lot of those posters went up before we had to change it. It was going to be Sunday the second, but the council's resurfacing the coast road that weekend, so we've moved it back a week. It's now Sunday the ninth.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The ninth of November. That actually suits me better. And where does it start? Somebody at work told me it starts at the surf club.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: It always has done, but the surf club's being rebuilt at the moment, so this year we're starting from the lighthouse, right at the north end of the beach. The finish is still in Norfolk Park, though, so it's a point-to-point course rather than a loop.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The lighthouse. That should be a nice view, at least. And how much does it cost to enter?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: That depends. For the general public it's forty-five dollars, but club members get a decent discount, so for members it's thirty.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Sorry, thirteen?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: I wish! No, thirty, three-oh. So if you join before you enter, you save fifteen dollars straight away.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Well, that's another good reason to join. And which charity does the money go to?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Last year it was the animal shelter, and the year before that it went to the surf lifesaving club. This year the committee voted for the local hospice. A few of our members have had family there, so it means a lot to people.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: That's a really good cause. And, er, how does it work on the day? Do I pick up my number at the start?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: That's how we used to do it, but the queues were terrible and people were missing the start. So now you collect your race pack the day before, on the Saturday, from the marina office, down by the boat ramp. It's open from nine till four.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: The marina office. So nothing's given out on the Sunday morning?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Nothing at all, so don't leave it till the last minute. There is a bag drop at the lighthouse, though, and we drive all the bags back to the park for you.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Great. And is there anything for people who finish? A medal, or...?

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Everyone gets a medal, yes. We used to hand out T-shirts as well, but to be honest, hardly anybody wore them, so this year every finisher gets a towel instead. A proper beach towel, with the race logo on it.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: A towel. That's actually useful, especially round here.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: That was the idea. Oh, and there are two water stations on the course, at three and seven kilometres, so you won't need to carry a bottle.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: Brilliant. Right, I'll come along to the pavilion on Tuesday, then, and join properly.

transcript.speaker: Jodie
transcript.text: Perfect. Don't forget your photo, and say hello to Gail. She'll look after you.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: I will. Thanks very much, Jodie. Bye.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

items.title: Outdoor Education Week
items.context: A primary school head teacher briefs parents at an evening meeting about the Year Six outdoor education week.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming out on such a wet night. I know some of you have come straight from work, so I'll try to keep this brisk. As you know, we're here to talk about the Year Six outdoor education week, which takes place in the first week of June.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Some of you will remember that when the school first started these trips, about ten years ago, the main idea was simply to get children more active. And fitness is still a very welcome side effect, of course. Other parents have said to me that it's a useful step towards secondary school, and I'd agree that it helps with that.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: But what the staff and I really want from the week this year is for the children to learn to manage without us. To pack their own bags, keep track of their own kit, and make decisions in their groups without an adult jumping in to sort everything out. That's harder than it sounds, for them and for us.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Now, some practical details. We're going back to Brackenside, the centre in mid-Wales that we used last year, so a lot of the staff already know the site well. The children will again be in activity groups of eight, each with its own instructor. We did ask whether the groups could be cut to six, but the centre simply couldn't staff that.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: What has changed is that, rather than coming home on the Wednesday as they did last year, the children will stay a second night and come back on the Thursday afternoon. The feedback we had was that one night was over almost before it had begun.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: The cost this year is two hundred and ten pounds. I know several families asked whether there's a reduction when brothers and sisters, or twins, go together. I'm afraid the centre doesn't offer one. The coach isn't part of that figure, either. The parents' association has very generously agreed to pay for it this year.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: What we can do is let you split the payment into three equal parts, in March, April and May, rather than paying it all at once. Just let the office know which you'd prefer. And if the cost is a real difficulty for any family, please come and talk to me privately. Nobody will miss out for that reason.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Mobile phones. Last year, as some of you will recall, we let the children bring them. They were collected when we arrived and handed back for half an hour each evening. Honestly, it caused far more homesickness than it cured. So this year, please don't pack a phone at all. If you need to reach your child, ring the centre, and we'll put photos on the school blog every evening.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 15 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 15 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Let me run through the activities now, because each one needs something slightly different from you. On the first full day there's cycling, in the morning. Helmets and bikes are provided by the centre, and the children will be back in plenty of time for lunch. However, part of the route goes along a quiet public lane, so this is the one activity the centre won't let a child take part in without your signature on the permission slip.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: Then canoeing, on the lake. Everyone is given a wetsuit and a buoyancy aid, so they don't need extra clothes for that. But their feet will get soaked, without exception, so they'll need a second pair of trainers or old shoes to change into afterwards, otherwise they'll be squelching about all day.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: The pond and stream study comes next. Some parents asked if the children should bring a torch, for looking under rocks and so on. They don't need one. What I would say is that the mud at Brackenside is a peculiar shade of orange, and it does not wash out. Please send them in something old that you won't mind putting straight in the bin afterwards.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: On the second evening, there's a night walk up through the woods, which the children always love. The centre used to lend out lamps for this, but they've stopped doing that now. So every child must bring a torch of their own. It doesn't need to be anything fancy, and please, not one that flashes.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: The orienteering day is the longest one. The groups are out in Gwern Forest from morning until late afternoon, which is too far to come back to the centre, so for once the kitchen won't be providing a hot lunch. Please make sure your child has sandwiches and a drink with them that morning. You might think they'd need sun cream, being out all day, but the centre has huge supplies, so please don't send any.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: And finally, climbing, on the indoor wall. The children's harnesses are all checked by the instructors, so you needn't worry about equipment. But the climbing centre insists, and this is their rule rather than ours, on having a list of any medicines a child takes, especially inhalers, before that session. If that applies to your child, please write it on the form that's going home tonight.

transcript.speaker: Mrs Hallam
transcript.text: One last thing. There's a small shop at Brackenside, and in the past children have taken pocket money. This year the shop will be closed for refurbishment, so they won't need any money at all. Right, I'll stop there. Are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

items.title: Commuting Survey Data
items.context: Two postgraduate students discuss the results of their survey into how people in the city commute and use public transport.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Right, Niamh, I've finally got all the responses into one spreadsheet. Four hundred and twelve in total.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Not bad at all. Fewer than we hoped, mind you. I think the questionnaire was just too long. Twelve pages was asking a lot of people. So, where did most of them come from in the end? Online?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: That's what I assumed too, given how much we pushed the link on social media. But no, the online version only got about a hundred and thirty. The paper copies did far better, and nearly all of those came from libraries.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Really? Not the doctors' surgeries?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: We got a grand total of nineteen from the surgeries. And the supermarkets wouldn't let us leave any in the first place, if you remember.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Oh yes, I remember the manager's face. And to think we spent a whole weekend designing that online version. Still, at least the paper ones were properly filled in. Half the online people gave up after page three.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Yeah, the completion rate on paper was much better. Anyway.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: OK. So, the big question. Why do the drivers say they don't use the buses? I'd have bet money it'd be the fares.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: So would I. But cost only came third. It isn't the price that puts them off, and it isn't really the journey time, which was second. By some distance, the thing drivers kept coming back to was reliability. Buses not turning up, or two arriving at once.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: That fits with the comments section, actually. People were furious about the number seven route. What about the cyclists? I was expecting pages about dangerous traffic.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: There was some of that, and a fair few mentioned showers at work. But the real complaint wasn't safety on the roads at all. It was that there's nowhere to leave a bike. They want secure storage, at the station and at work, because so many of them have had bikes stolen.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Right. And the over-sixties? I suppose price doesn't matter much to them, since most of them travel free.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Exactly, cost hardly featured. And interestingly, speed wasn't a big deal either. When we asked them to rank things, they put comfort above journey time almost every time. Getting a seat, a smooth ride, that sort of thing. Which surprised me a bit, actually. I'd assumed reliability would top their list as well, the same as it did for the drivers, but it only came third for them.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: That's a nice finding. Now, presentation. Doctor Ellis said tables, didn't she?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: She did say tables were fine for the appendix. And I'd started doing bar charts for everything.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: But so much of this is about where people live. I really think the main findings should go on maps. You'd see the gaps in the bus network straight away.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Yeah... you're right. Maps for the main results, then. I'll ditch the bar charts.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen and answer Questions 26 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: We need to be honest about the sample, though. Doctor Ellis will go straight for it.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: I know. My worry's the young people. I thought we'd hardly have any under twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: We're actually fine there, they're about twenty-two per cent, which is close to the city as a whole. And before you say it, students aren't a problem either. There were only about forty of them.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: No, you're right. The thing that does bother me is the postcodes. Nearly two thirds of the responses are from the eastern side of the city, because that's where the libraries we used are.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: That's the real weakness, isn't it? We can't say much about the west at all.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Agreed. What about the working-from-home question? A lot of people have said that's the most surprising part of the data.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: I don't think it surprised anyone, to be honest. It's what every report's been saying for years. My problem with it is the wording. We asked how often people work remotely, and half of them didn't know whether to count a morning at home as a day or not. You can see they've interpreted it in completely different ways.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Would it have helped if it had come earlier, before people got tired?

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: I don't think where it was made any difference. It's the way we phrased it.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Fair enough. Now, the follow-up interviews. You know I was against putting them in at first.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: You said eight interviews weren't worth the paper.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: I did. And it wasn't Doctor Ellis who changed my mind, either, although she did suggest them. And they certainly don't fix the response rate, eight people isn't going to do that. It's that they make sense of those odd figures for the occasional bus users, the ones who say they hate the buses and use them anyway. The interviews show why.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Great, so they're in. And the national census figures? I'd love to use them to back up our main argument.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: The trouble is their categories don't match ours. They lump cycling and walking together, for one thing. And they're from four years ago, before all the changes to the bus routes, so any comparison would be a bit misleading.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Hmm. I don't want to bin them completely, though. They took ages to find.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: How about we stick them at the back, as supporting material, but don't build anything on them?

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: OK, an appendix it is. So, before we see Doctor Ellis on Friday... should we email the bus company for their passenger numbers?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: They'd take weeks to reply. And there's no time to set up more interviews either.

transcript.speaker: Niamh
transcript.text: Then let's go back through the written comments. I noticed we've coded some of them differently from each other, so we should sort that out first.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Good idea. I'll take the first half, you take the second, and we can compare notes on Thursday evening. Then at least we'll walk in on Friday agreeing with each other.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

items.title: How Suspension Bridges Carry Loads
items.context: An engineering lecturer explains how suspension bridges are built, how they carry loads, and the problems caused by wind, pedestrians and corrosion.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the engineering of suspension bridges. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Okay, let's get started. Today we're looking at suspension bridges, which, for the longest spans, are still pretty much the only option we have. I want to focus on how they actually carry loads, and then on what can go wrong.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Just to put that in context: a good concrete beam bridge might span a couple of hundred meters between supports, and a cable-stayed bridge perhaps a thousand. The longest suspension bridges now cross more than two kilometers in a single span. So whatever they're doing, they're doing it very efficiently, and the reason comes down to how each part shares the work.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The basic idea is simple. The deck, the part you drive on, hangs from vertical cables, and those vertical cables hang from two main cables that run over the tops of the towers. Now, a lot of students assume the main cables are being squeezed by all that weight. They aren't. A cable can't resist being squeezed at all. The main cables are only ever in tension. They're being pulled. It's the towers that work in compression, pushing the load straight down into the foundations.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So where does the pull in the cables end up? At each end of the bridge, the cables are tied into anchorages. These are enormous blocks, and their whole job is to be heavy enough not to be dragged toward the river. On older bridges, they were built of masonry, cut stone, and in a few places the cables were simply anchored into solid rock. But today, almost without exception, anchorages are made of concrete, sometimes hundreds of thousands of tons of it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The main cables themselves are fascinating. You might picture a giant twisted rope, like a ship's hawser. That's not how it's done. Each cable is made of thousands of thin, parallel steel wires, and they're laid in place one at a time, high above the water, by a wheel running backward and forward between the anchorages. The process looks a bit like weaving, but engineers call it spinning, and it can take more than a year.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's think about the shape of the cable. If you hang a chain between two points, with nothing attached, it forms a curve called a catenary. You'll see that word in older textbooks applied to bridges. But a suspension bridge cable isn't just hanging under its own weight. Once the deck is attached, and the load is spread evenly along the span, the curve is much closer to a parabola. And that's the shape designers actually work with.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Here's a detail I love. On the very longest bridges, the towers aren't exactly parallel. They're a few centimeters farther apart at the top than at the bottom. It's not a construction error, and it's not the cables pulling them outward either. It's because each tower points toward the center of the Earth, so the curvature of the planet means they lean very slightly away from each other.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, what can go wrong? The big enemy is wind. You've probably all seen the film of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in nineteen forty, twisting until it fell apart. You'll often read that it was destroyed by resonance, like a singer shattering a glass. That's not really accurate. Engineers now agree the cause was flutter, a self-feeding twisting motion, where the movement of the deck changes the airflow, which then makes the movement bigger.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: After Tacoma, the first response was to make decks far stiffer. Designers didn't change the shape much at first. Instead, they hung deep trusses underneath the road, a kind of open steel framework, which stopped the deck from twisting. Later, especially in Europe, engineers went the other way, with slim box decks shaped rather like an aircraft wing, which they test in wind tunnels before anything is built. Both approaches work, but the wing-shaped decks use far less steel.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Wind isn't the only problem, though. People can be one too. When London's Millennium Bridge opened in two thousand, which is a very shallow suspension bridge, it started swaying from side to side. Pedestrians unconsciously fell into step with the movement, which made it worse. The bridge was closed, and there was talk of closing it for good, or rebuilding it entirely. In the end, the fix was to install dampers, devices that absorb the energy of the motion, a bit like the shock absorbers in a car.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, maintenance. You might expect the biggest long-term worry to be metal fatigue, the gradual weakening from millions of loading cycles. In fact, for main cables, that's a relatively minor issue. The real threat is corrosion. Water gets in between the wires, and once they start to rust, they snap, one at a time, deep inside the cable where nobody can see them.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So how do you find a broken wire you can't see? One method is to unwrap sections of cable and inspect them by eye, but that's slow and very expensive. X-rays have been tried, but the cables are just too thick. What many bridges use now is acoustic monitoring. Microphones are clamped along the cable, and when a wire breaks, it gives off a sharp crack, and the system records exactly where and when it happened.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some bridges go further and blow dry air through the cables to stop corrosion before it starts, and we'll look at those systems next week. For now, I'd like you to read the case study on the reading list before Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.

items.title: Renting a Flat
items.context: A young woman phones a letting agency to register as a tenant and hear about three flats that might suit her.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 1. You will hear a young woman phoning a letting agency about renting a flat. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Good morning, Calder Lettings, Daniel speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Oh, hi. Um, I filled in the form on your website last week about renting a one-bedroom flat, but nobody's got back to me, so I thought I'd just ring.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Ah, sorry about that, we've had a bit of a backlog. Let me take your details again and I'll set you up properly on our system. Can I have your name?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: It's Megan Rennison.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Megan... and that's R... E... N... I... S... O... N?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Nearly. Rennison has a double N. So R... E... double N... I... S... O... N.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Double N. Got it, thanks. And what do you do, Megan? The landlords always ask about employment.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Sure. Well, until the spring I was a receptionist at a dental surgery, and people still assume I'm a dental nurse, but I've actually just qualified as a paramedic. I started with the ambulance service in May.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Oh, well done. And when are you hoping to move in?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: So, my current tenancy ends on the thirty-first of July, but I don't want to rush into anything, so I'll stay with my sister for a bit. Um... she's away herself until the middle of August, so... I'd say from the twenty-third of August. Not before that.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The twenty-third. That's good timing, actually. A lot of our flats come free around then. Now, what's your budget per month?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Well, on the online form I put nine hundred pounds...

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Mm-hm.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: ...but I've been looking around, and I don't think I'll find anything decent for that. So I could stretch to nine hundred and fifty. I really can't go any higher than that, though.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That's realistic for this area. Is that including bills?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: No, that's just the rent. I'll pay the bills on top.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Fine. Just so you know, there's a holding deposit of one week's rent when you apply, and then a full deposit of five weeks' rent before you move in. We'll also need a reference from your current landlord.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: That's no problem. I've always paid on time, so she's happy to write one.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Great. And is there anything the landlord would need to agree to? Any special requirements?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Yes, er, I've got a pet. Not a dog. Everyone assumes that. And it isn't a cat either, I know landlords worry about their carpets. It's a rabbit. She lives indoors, in a big cage.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: A rabbit. That shouldn't put most of them off, but I'll make a note so there are no surprises. Right. I've got three flats on my list at the moment that might suit you. Shall I tell you about them?

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Yes, please. Hang on, let me find a pen... OK, go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: OK. The first one's on Mill Lane, near the park. The rent is eight hundred and seventy-five a month, so that's well within your budget.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Oh, nice. What floor is it on? I'd rather not be on the ground floor, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Well, the advert says second floor, but actually, that's wrong. I went round there on Monday, and it's on the third floor. It's the top of the building, so it gets a lot of light.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: That sounds lovely. Is there a catch?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The main thing is that there's no lift, so you'd be climbing three flights of stairs every day. Parking's fine, there's a residents' permit scheme, and the boiler was replaced last year.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Three flights with the shopping... and the rabbit's cage. Hmm. OK, what's the second one?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That's on Carlton Road, just by the station. Nine hundred and thirty a month. It's been completely refurbished, so...

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Completely?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Well... not quite. The bathroom wasn't touched, that's about ten years old, and the carpets are the same. But there's a brand-new kitchen, it was fitted just last month, and it's beautifully designed.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: That's a big plus, I cook a lot. But is it noisy, being so close to the station?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That's what everyone asks. Actually, the trains aren't the issue, the windows are all double-glazed. The problem is that the flat is directly above a bakery, and they start work at about four in the morning. You'd wake up to the smell of fresh bread, but you'd also hear the ovens and the delivery vans.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: With my shifts, I'm sometimes up at four anyway. And the third?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The third is in Orchard Court, the new development by the river. That's nine hundred and ninety, so a bit over...

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Yes, that's more than I said I could pay.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: I know, but it might be worth a look, because the landlord's said he may come down a little. It hasn't got a garden. There used to be a shared one, but it's been turned into car parking. But there's a really large balcony, big enough for a table and chairs, and it gets the sun all afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Oh, I'd love some outdoor space. Is there any storage?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Plenty. Each flat has its own storeroom in the basement.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: OK. Could I see all three? Maybe Carlton Road first, because of the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Of course. I could do Thursday afternoon, say two o'clock, and then go straight on to the other two.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Ah, I'm on a late shift on Thursday. Friday morning would be better.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Friday at ten, then. I'll meet you outside the bakery, and I'll text you the details this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Megan
transcript.text: Perfect. Thanks so much, Daniel.

items.title: A New Exhibition of Historical Maps
items.context: A museum curator introduces a group of visitors to a new exhibition of historical maps and explains the layout of the gallery.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 2. You will hear a museum curator talking to a group of visitors about a new exhibition. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Harland Museum. My name's Ruth Calloway, and I'm the curator of our new exhibition, Lines on the Land, which brings together five centuries of maps. Before you go in, I'd like to tell you a little about how it came about, and how the gallery is laid out.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: A lot of people assume the exhibition was planned to celebrate the museum's two-hundredth anniversary. It wasn't. That's not until next year. And while we did receive a very generous gift of sea charts from the Whitlock family last spring, those had already been earmarked for a separate display.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: The real starting point was rather more dramatic. Three years ago, builders were renovating the east wing, and behind some old wooden panelling they found a rolled-up estate map, almost perfectly preserved. Everything you'll see today grew out of the questions that map raised.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Now, most map exhibitions tell the story in date order, from the oldest to the newest, and we did consider doing that. In the end, though, we decided to group the maps according to what they were made for. So there are maps for war, maps for trade, maps for religious pilgrimage, and so on. It means a sixteenth-century chart can hang next to a twentieth-century one, which some visitors find a little disorienting at first.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: We'd also hoped to have material from every continent, but sadly two of our loans, from Australia and from Brazil, fell through at the last minute, so the collection is more European than I'd have liked.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Let me mention one map in particular. The oldest piece in the show is a map of a river valley drawn by a monk called Brother Anselm. We're in the unusual position of knowing exactly who made it, because he wrote his name in the corner. You'll notice some water stains, and there's a popular story that it survived a flood at the abbey. In fact, the stains came from a leaking roof in a Victorian library, much more recently.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: What's really exciting is that for decades it was catalogued as a fifteenth-century map. When we analysed the ink last year, it turned out to be nearly two hundred years older than anyone had thought.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: I'd strongly suggest you pick up an audio guide at the desk. It isn't free, I'm afraid, there's a charge of three pounds. We'd planned to include interviews with descendants of some of the mapmakers, but that part hasn't been recorded yet. What the guide does brilliantly, though, is decode all the little pictures and signs on the maps, which most of us simply can't read today.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Photography is allowed throughout, but please switch off your flash. Some of the inks are extremely sensitive to light, which is also why the gallery is kept rather dim. Your eyes will adjust after a minute or two, I promise.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: And a couple of changes since we first advertised the exhibition. We originally said you'd have to book tickets online in advance, but demand has been manageable, so you can just turn up. Children under twelve still pay a reduced price, by the way. They don't get in free. And the late opening, which was going to be on Thursdays, will now be on Fridays, until nine.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Right, let me explain the layout. If you look at the plan in your leaflet, you'll see the entrance at the bottom, and as you come in, the ticket desk is immediately on your right.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Go past the desk and right into that corner, and you'll find the Whitlock sea charts. You might expect them to be along the right-hand wall by the windows, but the light would fade the colours, so they're tucked away in the corner instead.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: In the centre of the room, you can't miss the giant globe. The interactive map table was originally going to stand between the entrance and the globe, but it caused queues right at the door. So it's now on the far side of the globe, between the globe and the doorway to the shop.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Along the left-hand wall there are two large cases. The one nearest the entrance holds our Roman road maps. The estate map, the one the builders found, is in the second case along, halfway down that wall.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: In the top left-hand corner you'll see the staircase up to the library. There's a short film about how maps were engraved and printed, and that's shown on a screen just to the right of the stairs as you face them. Not underneath them. That space is only used for storage.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Just to the left of the shop doorway is where the children's trail begins, and you'll probably hear it before you see it. And halfway along the window wall there's a row of benches, if you need a rest, with a lovely view of the river.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: And finally, our replica printing press. We'd hoped to put it in the middle of the window wall, but the floor there isn't strong enough to take the weight. So it's in the top right-hand corner, to the right of the shop doorway. Our volunteers give demonstrations every hour. Right, do enjoy the exhibition, and do come and find me if you have any questions.

items.title: A Presentation on Bioplastics
items.context: An environmental science student discusses a draft of his presentation on bioplastics with his tutor.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 3. You will hear a student called Liam talking to his tutor about a presentation he is preparing on bioplastics. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 26.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Come in, Liam, have a seat. So, the bioplastics presentation. How's it coming along?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah, not bad. I've got a full draft, but I wanted to run through the section on the different sources with you before I finalise the slides.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Good idea. Go on, then.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: So I start with corn starch, because it's still the most widely used. And I'd written that the big problem with it is that it's brittle, you know, it cracks easily...

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Hmm, I'd be careful there. That was true of the early versions, but the blends they use now are surprisingly tough. And you've got a line here about toxic by-products. I couldn't find any reliable source for that.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Fair enough, I think I got that off a blog. So really it comes down to the fact that every hectare of maize grown for plastic is a hectare that isn't feeding anyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Exactly. That's the argument you should lead with.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Then sugarcane. Now, I went in thinking this was the worst of the lot, because you hear so much about rainforest being cleared for plantations.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: And?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Well, the more I read, the more I realised that's mostly a myth, at least where plastics are concerned. Most of it's made from bagasse, the fibre that's left over once the sugar's been extracted, so it doesn't need any extra land at all. I reckon it gets a lot of stick that it really doesn't deserve.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: I'd go along with that. And it's cheap to process, which helps.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Seaweed's my favourite, honestly. I assumed supply would be the sticking point, since wild seaweed can only be harvested at certain times...

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: But it's farmed now, isn't it? All year round.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly, so that's not an issue. And it's strong enough for most packaging. The trouble is, it still costs about four times as much to make as ordinary plastic, and until that comes down, no manufacturer's going to touch it.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Sadly, I think you're right.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Then there's the one made from used cooking oil, collected from restaurants.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Ah yes. I find that one rather appealing. The oil's a waste product, so it ought to be cheap.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: It is, the cost's fine. But the bags they trialled apparently kept a faint whiff of chips, which isn't ideal if you're wrapping, I don't know, a birthday cake.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: No, quite. Make sure you mention that.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Next is chitosan, which comes from shrimp and crab shells. People expect it to smell of fish...

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: And doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: No, it's completely odourless once it's been processed. And it's tough. The problem is that the shells only come in while the fishing season's open, so for months on end there's nothing to work with.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: So the factories would be sitting idle half the year. Yes, that's a real limitation.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: And the last one is potato peel, from crisp factories.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: I'd have thought the supply there was enormous.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: It is. They run all year, so there's no shortage, and it isn't expensive either. But the material just doesn't hold up. It tears really easily, so you couldn't use it for anything heavier than, say, a sandwich wrapper.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: That's fair. Just make that point clearly. Oh, and one more thing before we move on. Are you going to explain the difference between biodegradable and compostable? Because a lot of your audience will assume they're the same.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Ah. I hadn't planned to, no. I suppose I could add a slide near the start, saying that compostable means it breaks down within a set time, but usually only in an industrial facility, not a garden heap.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Yes, do. Otherwise half your argument won't make sense to them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 27 to 30.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Remind me, what made you pick this topic in the first place? Was it your summer job?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: At the packaging firm in Brisbane? No, I was only stacking boxes there, I never saw how anything was made. And I'd actually put down ocean plastics as my first choice, and nobody else had chosen it, so I could easily have kept it. It was a documentary about compostable coffee cups that changed my mind. I watched it one night and just couldn't stop thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Well, it shows. Now, the slides. You've got twelve for fifteen minutes, which is about right, so don't worry about the number.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: I was worried I'd crammed too much writing onto them.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Actually, no, you've been quite disciplined, it's mostly key words. My concern is the graphs. The labels are tiny and the colours are almost identical, so from the back of a lecture theatre no one will be able to make them out.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Right. I'll redo those. And for the opening, I was going to hit them with a statistic, like how many million tonnes of plastic get made every year.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Everyone does that, and the numbers are so huge they don't mean anything to people.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Or I could put a question to the audience. Like, who here has used a compostable cup this week?

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: That can fall rather flat if nobody answers. What about the thing you told me last week? When you buried a so-called biodegradable cup in your garden and dug it up six months later?

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: And it looked brand new.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Exactly. Start there. It happened to you, it's memorable, and it leads straight into your argument.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: OK, yeah, I'll do that. And the conclusion? I wondered whether it's a bit short.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Short is no bad thing at the end. And you haven't brought in any new material, which is good, because people often do. But you never actually tell us what you think should happen. You list the pros and cons, and then you just stop.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: So I'm sitting on the fence.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis
transcript.text: Firmly. Give them a clear recommendation, even if it's a cautious one.

transcript.speaker: Liam
transcript.text: Right. I'll argue that seaweed deserves the research funding. That's what I actually believe, anyway.

transcript.text: Then there's the one made from used cooking oil, collected from restaurants.

transcript.speaker: Dr Hollis

items.title: The Domestication of the Horse
items.context: An archaeology lecturer explains how new evidence has changed ideas about where and when the horse was domesticated.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the domestication of the horse. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at one of the most consequential partnerships in human history, the one between people and horses. It's a story that has been substantially rewritten in the last decade or so, largely thanks to genetics, so some of what you'll find in older textbooks is, frankly, out of date. I'll start with the evidence that was traditionally used, then turn to what the DNA tells us, and finish with how the horse spread.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For a long time, the strongest candidate for the first horse-keeping society was the Botai culture, in what is now northern Kazakhstan, around three thousand five hundred BCE. The Botai were clearly obsessed with horses. At some of their settlements, horse bones make up more than ninety per cent of all the animal remains.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Of course, huge numbers of bones might simply mean very successful hunting. So researchers looked for evidence that the animals were controlled. The first line of evidence came not from the legs or the spine, where you might expect to see signs of heavy work, but from the teeth. Some Botai horses had small areas of wear on their premolars, which was interpreted as damage from a bit, the piece of equipment placed in a horse's mouth to steer it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second line of evidence was chemical. Researchers analysed residues left inside Botai pottery. Now, if these people were hunters, you'd expect fats from horse meat, and that wasn't what made the headlines. What was significant was the presence of fats from mare's milk. And you can't milk a wild horse, or at least, not twice.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Thirdly, there's the question of whether horses were kept in enclosures. Excavators had found rings of post holes, but these were ambiguous, as they could equally be the remains of houses. Much more persuasive were unusually high levels of nitrogen and phosphorus in the soil within certain areas, which is what you'd get from large quantities of dung accumulating in a pen.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So the case for Botai looked strong. Then, in two thousand and eighteen, a genetic study sequenced the DNA of Botai horses, and the results were a real surprise. They were not the ancestors of the horses we ride today. Instead, they were the ancestors of the Przewalski horse, the stocky animal found on the Mongolian steppe.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: This had an awkward consequence. Przewalski's horse had always been celebrated as the last truly wild horse on Earth. That description can no longer stand. If its ancestors were kept by the Botai, then Przewalski's horses are feral, that is, descended from domesticated animals that escaped human control and returned to life in the wild. Incidentally, by the late nineteen-sixties they had disappeared from the wild altogether, and every one alive today is descended from a handful of animals kept in zoos.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That left an obvious question. If modern domestic horses didn't come from Botai, where did they come from? Over the years, various regions had been proposed, including Anatolia, in modern Turkey, and the Iberian Peninsula. A very large study published in two thousand and twenty-one, which analysed the genomes of hundreds of ancient horses, finally gave an answer: the western steppe, around the lower reaches of the Volga and Don rivers, in what is now southern Russia, at roughly two thousand two hundred BCE.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The same study identified genes that seem to have been strongly selected by those early breeders. You might expect speed to have been a priority. It wasn't, at least not at first. One of the genes is associated with a stronger back, which would have made the animals better able to carry riders and loads.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Another is linked to more docile behaviour. Wild horses are prey animals and they panic easily. An animal that was less fearful, and therefore less likely to bolt or kick, would have been far more valuable to its owners than one that was simply bigger or faster.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's a further clue in how quickly generations succeeded each other. Around this time, the average interval between a horse's birth and the birth of its offspring fell to roughly half its previous length. This isn't something that happens naturally. It only really makes sense if people were deliberately controlling breeding, choosing which animals mated, and when.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, the genetic evidence has also forced us to revisit the role of the Yamnaya people, who spread from the steppe into Europe from about three thousand BCE. There's a dramatic image, which you'll still find in popular books, of Yamnaya warriors galloping westwards on horseback.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Unfortunately for that picture, the horses found at the relevant sites don't belong to the modern domestic lineage at all. What seems to have made the Yamnaya so mobile was not riding, but heavy wagons, drawn by oxen, which allowed whole families to move with their possessions.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Once the modern domestic horse had emerged, though, it spread extraordinarily fast, reaching Anatolia, central Europe and much of Asia within a few centuries after two thousand BCE. What drove that expansion? Not cavalry. Mounted warfare on any real scale comes considerably later. The key development was the chariot, a light, fast vehicle with spoked wheels, which turned the horse into a weapon of enormous prestige.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So, to sum up. The Botai story isn't wrong, exactly, because the Botai clearly did manage horses in some way. But they turned out to be a side branch rather than the main trunk of the family tree. It's a useful reminder that archaeological evidence which seems to point clearly in one direction can be overturned very quickly by a new technique. Next week, we'll look at what happened when horses reached the Americas.
